entries.title: India news: Activists decry AI surveillance at CJP protests
entries.summary: A suit has been brought alleging mass surveillance and data collection of "Cockroach" movement protestors. DW has more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: Activists decry AI surveillance at CJP protests

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 28, 2026

A suit has been brought alleging mass surveillance and data collection of "Cockroach" movement protestors. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A student activist has appealed Delhi's High Court to declare mass surveillance of protesters ​unconstitutional
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta defended the Indian police's conduct during the CJP protest
  • The Assam and Bihar governments have agreed to drop charges against some protesters

Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, July 28:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Modi government faces challenge from activists over AI use at CJP protest

Modi government faces challenge from activists over AI use at CJP protest

Activists in India have challenged Narendra Modi's government over the use of AI-powered surveillance during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest. 

The controversy erupted when protesters and media reports showed a police surveillance van equipped with cameras on a telescopic mast providing a 360-degree view of the gathering.

Student activist Aishe Ghosh has asked the Delhi High Court to declare mass surveillance of protesters ​unconstitutional.

She also wants the court to order the destruction of all personal data collected during the CJP demonstration.

India has no law governing the use of facial recognition technology by police and surveillance ​at the main protest site in New Delhi was a breach of the law, activists say.

During the case's hearing, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta defended the Indian police conduct, saying privacy claims at a public gathering were "ironical" and the checks were "absolutely necessary" and "in legitimate state interest."

entries.title: Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the United States to press for stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine seeks air defense systems

July 28, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the United States to press for stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the United States ahead of talks with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying Kyiv's top priority was securing stronger air defense and strategic cooperation as Russia intensified attacks.

"Our number-one priority is anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation with America. Peace needs to be brought closer," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after arriving in the US.

The two leaders are due to meet at the White House before attending a tribute to Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who passed away earlier this month.

US-Ukraine ties improving

The long-strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have improved in recent weeks.

Since returning to office in January last year, Trump largely stopped direct US arms shipments to Ukraine, instead allowing European allies to buy American weapons and supply them to Kyiv.

However, Washington remains a key ally, providing intelligence and access to the Starlink satellite network used by Ukrainian frontline troops to communicate.

In a sign of improving ties, Trump, in a meeting with Zelenskyy in Turkey earlier this month, pledged to help Ukraine produce Patriot air defense systems, saying Kyiv would be able to produce them "pretty quickly."

This has been a long-running request from Kyiv in order to counter Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes

The Trump-Zelenskyy meeting comes as more than four years have passed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war, both sides have stepped up long-range strikes.

Russia said on Tuesday that more than 390 Ukrainian drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, damaging residential buildings.

Russian state media also reported that Russian forces struck two vessels, including a ship in the Black Sea that Moscow claimed was transporting military supplies for Ukraine, according to Reuters.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Heat wave threatens to worsen France, Spain wildfires
entries.summary: A fresh spell of extreme heat, driven by climate change, is expected to intensify some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades, stretching firefighting resources.
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

A fresh spell of extreme heat, driven by climate change, is expected to intensify some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades, stretching firefighting resources.

A forecast of an incoming heat wave across France and Spain this week is threatening to hamper firefighting efforts as some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades rage on.

France's weather service forecast temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) from Tuesday, while Spain's AEMET warned of a new heat wave from Wednesday till the end of the week, with highs of 42 degree Celsius in the northeast and 39 degrees Celsius in central regions.

Authorities said soaring temperatures, dry winds and low humidity would push wildfire danger to "extreme" levels, even as forests turned tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year.

Thousands of firefighters and water-dropping aircraft raced to contain the blazes before temperatures rise further.

Experts linked the scale of the fires to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves driven by climate change, as hotter and drier conditions are making wildfires more destructive.

Macron warns of 'hard' times

In France, President Emmanuel Macron said one fire in the Landes region had been contained, but a much larger wildfire near Bordeaux continued to burn after scorching about 42,000 hectares, forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate and destroying hundreds of homes.

"The weeks ahead will be hard. We must hold firm," Macron said.

Overnight on Tuesday, firefighters prevented a massive wildfire along the Atlantic coast west of Bordeaux from spreading, authorities said.

According to officials, 93 firefighters have been injured since the operation began.

Aid from Germany arrived in the region on Monday in the form of two transport helicopters and an A400M transport aircraft carrying equipment.

In Spain, wildfires west of Madrid and in other regions have forced about 60,000 people to flee.

With the coming heat wave threatening to fuel further spread of the wildfires, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska firefighters in Spain made progress after a "positive night" against wildfires to the west of Madrid.

"It has been a reasonably positive night, thanks to the tremendous effort of all the public emergency services," Grande-Marlaska said. "We are in critical hours."



Some 150,000 hectares of land have burned in Spain and 115,000 hectares in France since the start of this year.

At a campsite near Navaluenga, west of the capital, ravaged by Spain's worst wildfire on record, the site co-owner Maria Angeles Canete said her family lost everything.

"We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing," she told the AFP news agency.

EU firefighting resources stretched thin

The European Union deployed additional firefighting aircraft to France, while EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib warned that resources are under growing strain as extreme fire conditions spread across southern and central Europe.

"Extreme conditions are looming for Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in addition to France, the Iberian Peninsula... where the situation is expected to worsen, including in Portugal starting today," Lahbib said.

In Italy, a wildfire in the southern Puglia region forced the evacuation of hundreds of tourists from beaches and campgrounds, authorities said.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Iran war: Netanyahu in Washington for meeting with Trump
entries.summary: The meeting between the US President and the Israeli Prime Minister will be the first since the start of the war on Iran. Meanwhile, Iran has executed two men in relation to anti-government protests. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: Netanyahu in Washington for meeting with Trump

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 28, 2026

The meeting between the US President and the Israeli Prime Minister will be the first since the start of the war on Iran. Meanwhile, Iran has executed two men in relation to anti-government protests. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Benjamin Netanyahuarrives in Washington
  • Israeli PM set to meet President Trumpfor the first time since the start of the Iran war
  • Trump to also meet with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy
  • Iran executes two men in relation to January protests
  • US sets date for next Israel-Lebanontalks

Read below for the latest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Tuesday, July 28:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Iran discusses Strait of Hormuz with Oman, Saudi Arabia

Iran discusses Strait of Hormuz with Oman, Saudi Arabia

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi discussed the status of the Strait of Hormuz in separate phone calls with his Omani and Saudi Arabian counterparts on Tuesday.

A statement from the Iranian foreign ministry said Araqchi "emphasized the need to strengthen ​cooperation and advance joint ⁠diplomatic efforts to establish stability in the region, and lift the insecurity imposed ​on the Strait of Hormuz due to the aggressive actions of the United States."

An unnamed Gulf source told the Reuters news agency that Omani foreign minister Badr al-Busaidi had presented a proposal to Araqchi for a joint regional mechanism to manage the key waterway.

The proposal is reportedly based on the model used to regulate the Strait of Malacca between Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, which uses a system of voluntary fees to fund navigation, environmental ​protection and ‌search and rescue.

The proposal would ensure that Iran would not exercise sole control of the Strait of Hormuz and would therefore be potentially more palatable to the United States and other regional powers.

Skip next section Iran executes two men in relation to January protests

Iran executes two men in relation to January protests

The Iranian judiciary announced on Tuesday that two men convicted of acts of violence during anti-government protests in January had been hanged.

"The death sentences of Abolfazl Sepahi and Amir-Hossein Safari were carried out this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online portal said.

It said the pair had been found guilty of "attacking police officers with machetes and knives, tying them to road signs, pulling them on the ground, dousing them with gasoline, and setting them on fire."

Other charges, according to Mizan, included "moharebeh [waging war against God] by drawing weapons and creating fear and terror" and "corruption on earth for committing acts that severely disrupted public order and security in the country."

The Mehr news agency reported that the executions took place in "a square in the city of Malekshahr" in the central Isfahan province, in the presence of members of the public.

Two other men were hanged on similar charges in Isfahan province on July 19.

In December 2025, a protest movement initially sparked by the high cost of living in Iran rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" which they claimed were orchestrated by the United States and Israel, while rights groups based abroad maintain that security forces fired on protesters.

According to Amnesty International, Iran conducts the second most judicial executions of any country, after China.

Skip next section Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine, Iran conflicts overlap

Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine, Iran conflicts overlap

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also expected to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday, emphasizing the increasing overlaps between the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US war against Iran.

The meeting comes after Ukraine reportedly carried out long-range strikes against Iranian-linked vessels in the Caspian Sea over the weekend, which Zelenskyy claimed had been carrying military cargo linked to Iran.

Tehran confirmed that one of its ships had exploded in the attack, killing a sailor and injuring several others, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei warning that Ukraine's actions amounted to a "dangerous act of adventurism."

The common denominator in both conflicts, according to Kyiv, is Russia, which is separated from northern Iran by only a short sea route bypassing Azerbaijan in the Caspian Sea, or by a 250-kilometer (155-mile) strip of Azeri territory over land.

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy claimed that Moscow has been providing Tehran with satellite imagery of US bases in the Gulf region.

President Trump has played down the impact of any potential Russian assistance for Iran, telling reporters on Air Force One on Monday: "I don’t think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level. And if they have, it has been very un-impactful."

Other overlapping issues linking the wars in Ukraine and Iran include the stretching of US munitions stockpiles available for each theater and the cutting-edge Ukrainian experience in drone warfare, which Kyiv has been sharing with the US.

Skip next section US support for Iran war in decline — survey

US support for Iran war in decline — survey

Popular support for the United States' war with Iran has fallen to its lowest since the start of the conflict five months ago, according to a new survey conducted by the Reuters news agency and the Ipsos polling institute.

According to the poll, carried out over the weekend and published on Monday, only one third of US citizens remain supportive of their country's military operations.

Meanwhile, 69% are of the opinion that US President Donald Trump has failed to adequately explain the goals of the intervention.

A government spokeswoman told Reuters that the White House doesn't attach any meaning to the poll and that President Trump doesn't make decisions based on fluctuating survey results.

She insisted that the most important objective in the war against Iran remains the degradation of Tehran's ability to produce a nuclear weapon.

18 US service personnel have been killed during operations so far, in addition to thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon, despite Trump promising during his 2024 election campaign to keep the United States out of foreign wars.

The survey put general public support for Trump at 37%.

Skip next section Israel intercepts drone near Jordanian border

Israel intercepts drone near Jordanian border

The Israeli air force said on Tuesday morning that it had intercepted a drone close to the border with Jordan — although it provided no information regarding the potential provenance of the weapon.

According to the air force, the drone did not enter Israeli airspace.

The operation came following the interception of two further drones near the Jordanian border on Monday, the provenance of which also remains unclear.

In addition to Israeland the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Jordan also shares borders with Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, giving it a geographically important position amid several regional conflicts. The United States also maintains a military presence on Jordanian air force bases.

Although Israel took joint part in the initial offensive against Iran back in February, it has not participated in the most recent round of strikes.

Skip next section US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

The US State Department confirmed on Monday that the next round of talks between Israel and Lebanon would begin in Rome next week on August 4.

"In Rome, technical groups will focus on advancing the full implementation of the framework agreement," a State Department official told the French AFP news agency.

The Israel-Lebanon framework deal calls for an end to hostilities, the disarmament of militant group Hezbollah, the deployment of Lebanese military troops in the south of the country, and for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from Lebanon in two so-called "pilot zones."

The official said the agenda would include "resolving all outstanding border issues," among other things.

"The experience of the initial zones will help us perfect pilot-zone implementation so it can expand in a phased manner," the official added.

Despite the framework agreement, Lebanon has reported intermittent Israeli strikes and artillery shelling on the south of the country in recent days.

Skip next section Netanyahu lands in Washington to meet with Trump

Netanyahu lands in Washington to meet with Trump

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Washington on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump .

It will be Netanyahu's first visit to the White House since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, triggering the ongoing war.

"This is a great privilege, but it is also a great responsibility," Netanyahu said before departing Israel on Monday.

"We will discuss all the issues on the agenda, first and foremost Iran. Naturally, our goal is to safeguard our security and also to expand the circle of peace around us," he added.

The trip comes as Trump increasingly expresses frustration toward Netanyahu over hostilities in the Middle East, referring to him in one interview as a "difficult guy."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to discuss the conflict today with US President Donald Trump in Washington. The two leaders have publicly disagreed throughout the course of the war, with Trump in recent weeks expressing frustration with Netanyahu's actions in the Middle East.

Meanwhile, arrangements are being made for the next round of direct Israeli-Lebanese talks early next month, according to Washington.

Follow our blog for the latest updates.

entries.title: US singer D4vd to stand trial in killing of 14-year-old girl
entries.summary: D4vd is accused of murdering 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez in 2025. Prosecutors allege that he dismembered her body and drove around with her decomposing remains in his car.
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

D4vd is accused of murdering 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez in 2025. Prosecutors allege that he dismembered her body and drove around with her decomposing remains in his car.

Content warning: This article discusses child sexual abuse and murder.

A US judge ruled on Monday that there is enough evidence for singer D4vd to stand trial over the killing and dismembering of a 14-year-old girl with whom he had an illegal sexual relationship.

After prosecutors presented evidence over a five-day hearing, Los Angeles Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that the 21-year-old singer, whose real name is David Burke, would stand trial.

He faces multiple charges including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains. He has pleaded not guilty.

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said outside court that prosecutors are still deciding whether to seek the death penalty.

What are the allegations against D4vd?

In September 2025, the dismembered, decomposing body of 14-year-old year old Celeste Rivas Hernandez was found in the back of a Tesla that was registered in Burke's name.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke first met Rivas Hernandez when she was 11, and began sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18.

Los Angeles police detective Corey Farrell told the court under questioning that the parents of both Burke and Rivas Hernandez knew about their relationship and that her parents had given consent for her to travel to London with him for a week.

The detective also read text messages to the court in which Rivas Hernandez said she had fallen pregnant and had an abortion.

Around 24 hours before she was murdered, Rivas Hernandez sent Burke a series of expletive-laden text messages. Prosecutors said the text messages showed she was jealous of another woman and threatened to expose their illegal relationship.

The singer then allegedly paid for an Uber to bring Rivas Hernandez to his home where prosecutors said he stabbed her to death upon entering.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke then proceeded to immediately cover up the killing. Burke sent Rivas Hernandez multiple text messages asking where she was and expressing concern — messages which prosecutors say were sent as cover after he murdered her.

Meanwhile, prosecutors also pointed to Burke's online order receipts under a fictitious name, which showed he purchased chainsaws, a shovel and an inflatable pool.

He allegedly used the items to dismember her body in his garage, where DNA matching the victim was found on blood stains, according to prosecutors.

He also purchased a portable "burn box" incinerator that turned out to be too small to destroy her body, prosecutors said.

Burke then allegedly drove around for weeks with Rivas Hernandez's dismembered body in his trunk before the seemingly abandoned Tesla was ultimately towed to an impound lot in Hollywood.

Prosecutors reject accident claims

Prosecutor Beth Silverman told the court that "there's nothing in this case that sounds like an accident."

Burke's lawyer meanwhile said "there was no evidence of deliberate intention to kill."

Burke, performing as D4vd, gained a massive following on social media like TikTok and Soundcloud with his breakthrough track "Romantic Homicide" in 2022.

In April 2025, he played at the Coachella music festival and released his first album "Withered," two days after authorities say Rivas Hernandez was killed.

Edited by: Rana Taha

If you or someone you know are experiencing or have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help (https://lila.help) lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.

entries.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy in UK to meet new PM Burnham
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy traveled to Portsmouth for UK PM Andy Burnham's first meeting with a foreign leader since taking office. The UK pledged "unwavering support" in Ukraine's ongoing defense against Russia.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's Zelenskyy in UK to meet new PM Burnham

July 27, 2026

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy traveled to Portsmouth for UK PM Andy Burnham's first meeting with a foreign leader since taking office. The UK pledged "unwavering support" in Ukraine's ongoing defense against Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the UK on Monday where he and new prime minister Andy Burnhamdiscussed continued defense cooperation. The two visited some 200 Ukrainian service members training with UK troops at Portsmouth Naval Base.

The Ukrainian forces have been sharpening their war-fighting and countermining measures for operations in the Black Sea.

Speaking in Portsmouth, Burnham said, "Volodymyr, you are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office and that is no accident."

"It is intended to send a very clear message," the new prime minister added, "We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honor every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Posting on X after the meeting, Zelenskyy wrote: "We greatly appreciate that our team is the first to visit the United Kingdom since Andy Burnham took office. This is an important signal of support, and the Prime Minister assured us that this support remains unwavering."

UK providing new radar jamming technology to aid deep strike capabilities

Burnham announced that the UK is now providing Kyiv with access to its "Stone Cloak" electronic jamming technology, with thousands of the jammers already given to Kyiv according to Downing Street.

When affixed to drones, the battle-tested, tablet-sized Stone Cloak jammers can shield weapons from Russian air-defense systems detection, providing Kyiv with more lethal long-distance strike capabilities.

"Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries," Burnham said.

The deal comes as Ukraine has shifted from a purely defensive posture and increased its attacks on sites deep within Russia, notably its targeting of oil, military and logistics installations.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy told UK broadcaster Sky News that he hoped to sign a strong "drone deal" with Burnham to boost drone production capacity and technology sharing, adding, "we don't have enough missiles" to defend against Russia's continued air attacks.

Russia, said Zelenskyy, "can increase the production of ballistic missile missiles and that's why we need air defense as soon as possible."

UK support for Kyiv continues despite a revolving cast of prime ministers

Zelenskyy's visit is Burnham's first bilateral meeting with a foreign leader since taking over at Downing Street last week and comes as the Ukrainian prepares to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday.

Burnham assured Zelenskyy of the UK's "unwavering support" as Kyiv defends itself against a more than four-year Russian invasion.

"Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering," according to a statement.

"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine."

Zelenskyy described ties with the UK as "the strongest relationship in the entire history" of the two nations.

Prior to the meeting, Downing Street said Burnham — the fifth prime minister that Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched its unprovoked full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022 — would pledge "to continue the unbreakable bond between the two nations."

Downing Street on Monday said that the UK had provided some 25 billion pounds (€29 billion ,$33 billion) in assistance to Ukraine since the war began, 16 billion of which were given in direct military assistance.

Zelenskyy to meet with Trump

From the UK, Zelenskyy will travel to Washington, where he will meet with US President Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Support from Trump, who is currently bogged down in his own war with Iran, has wavered during his time in office and the two leaders have had a famously contentious relationship.

Trump did, however, recently announce that Kyiv could be given permission to build US Patriot missile systems as Russian air assaults continue unabated.

In his Sunday Sky News interview, Zelenskyy expressed understanding for Trump's predicament, saying, "I understand the United States is focussing on the Middle East," adding that he would, "try to manage it [the war in Ukraine] with some Europeans and with Americans and with some other countries."

"This," he said, is "a big challenge," both for himself and for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy did get an important bit of assistance from lawmakers in Washington recently when Congress advanced bipartisan legislation targeting countries purchasing Russian energy, potentially making it harder for the Kremlin and President Vladimir Putin to finance its ongoing war.

While in Washington, Zelenskyy is also expected to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a key proponent of US support for Ukraine who died unexpectedly earlier this month after returning from Kyiv.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Chad's government says it's withdrawing from the ICC
entries.summary: Chad's Foreign Ministry has announced plans to leave the International Criminal Court. It said that its effectiveness was "limited and uneven." Chad's leader is a military officer accused of repressing the opposition.
entries.content:
Chad

Chad's government says it's withdrawing from the ICC

July 27, 2026

Chad's Foreign Ministry has announced plans to leave the International Criminal Court. It said that its effectiveness was "limited and uneven." Chad's leader is a military officer accused of repressing the opposition.

Chad's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Monday saying that it had notified the UN Secretary General of its intention to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the international accord underpinning the International Criminal Court (ICC). 

Chad is the fourth francophone African country whose government is very closely linked to its miltary to take such a step in less than a year — following the coordinated exit by the juntas running Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger last September. 

The ICC prosecutes individuals for war crimes and crimes against humanity; it began operating in 2002.

What did Chad's government say about the ICC pullout?

The Foreign Ministry said that its decision followed "an in-depth review of the functioning of the International Criminal Court since it began operating in 2002 and of its record, whose effectiveness remains limited and uneven across different regions."

It said the court's own record of prosecutions revealed an "undeniable and egregious selectivity in principle, whether or not this selectivity is desired or subjected."

The statement then listed the ICC investigations launched since the court's founding, saying that nine of 13 cases concerned African states, while only four applied to other regions of the world and were "without any concrete progress" as yet.

It said that of seven individuals detained as a result of ICC investigations, only one hailed from a situation beyond the African continent.

The Foreign Ministry alleged that this demonstrated a lasting concentration of ICC cases focused on "the Global South in general and the African continent in particular." Chad also appealed to other African Union members to follow in its footsteps.

"This irrevocable decision by Chad in no way constitues a renunication of the moral imperative to provide justice to victims; rather, it reflects the conviction that national judicial systems and African judicial mechanisms are fully capable of carrying out this mission with dignity," the statement, signed by Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ibrahim Adam Mahamat, concluded.

What did Chad say about the US role in this move?

Last Thursday, Chad's Foreign Ministry had also raised the issue of the ICC.

In a statement after talks between a Chadian minister and a US official for Africa, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia Jr., the government in N'Djamena said the US had urged it to reconsider its ICC membership.

"The US side expressed its concerns about the functionality of this institution and desired that Chad reexamine its commitment to the Rome Statute," the ministry wrote. Chad said that it "indicated that this request would be examined by the responsible authorities."

The withdrawal coincides with last week's vote to dimiss the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

The US, like Russia and several other countries, never ratified the Rome Statute and fully signed up to the ICC. However, past administrations in Washington had been broadly supportive of the court's work.

This has changed in particular since the ICC's issued arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister, soon after Donald Trump won a second term in office in November 2024. The second Trump administration has often been critical both of the independent ICC and the UN more generally, under whose auspices the Rome Statute mechanism was negotiated. 

Why might Chad and President Mahamat Idriss Deby fear the ICC?

While Chad now has a nominally civilian government, the same family with close ties to the military has been in charge for more than 35 years.

Former President Idriss Deby came to power in a military coup in late 1990. He was in office for more than 30 years before the news of his death in April 2021. According to Chadian accounts, the former general died fighting on the front lines against an insurgency in the north of the country, just a day after news of his election victory for a sixth consecutive term had been announced after a vote marked by protests and widespread arrests.

His son, another officer, Mahamat Idriss Deby, was named the head of a transitional military council after Deby's death, with the government disbanded.

In October 2022, he extended his interim mandate, prompting public protests that were violently suppressed. Dozens were killed and several opposition parties were banned in response. 

By 2024, after a constitutional referendum, Mahamat Deby did stand in presidential elections. The main challenger still permitted to run was his own prime minsiter, Succes Masra, who had returned from exile in the US earlier that year. Deby the younger won with 60.1% of the vote, albeit with Masra and other opposition groups disputing the results.  Masra was arrested in May 2025, accused of inciting hatred amid violent clashes the government defined as an "attempted coup." He was sentenced to 20 years in prison last August. 

Chad is still fighting an insurgency lasting roughly a decade in the north of the country led by two groups with rear bases in southern Libya. It also faces an influx of refugees from Sudan's civil war and various other soures of domestic unrest.

The three other West African nations to pull out of the ICC last September — Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — are all under supposedly interim leadership by military juntas after a 2020 coup in Mali, a 2022 takeover in Burkina Faso and a 2023 coup in Niger.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet reshuffle
entries.summary: After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.
entries.content:
Germany

German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet reshuffle

July 27, 2026

After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.

On Monday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was finally able to announce the name of the new Federal Minister of Transport in Berlin, following a weekend of speculation and debate. Steffen Bilger (CDU), aged 47 — who previously served as a state secretary in the transport ministry from 2018 to 2021 — is stepping up to lead the ministry.

The Chancellor had criticized the outgoing Transport Minister, Patrick Schnieder (CDU), for doing too little to address the chronic chaos and frequent delays plaguing the Deutsche Bahn railway system. Merz also faulted him for initiating too few projects to improve Germany's ailing infrastructure.

On Monday, Merz said he expected the new minister to ensure that "we become faster and better at driving a new era of progress in Germany."

Bilger's appointment marks the latest step in a cabinet reshuffle of the conservative wing of the government. This chain reaction of personnel changes was triggered by the resignation of Jens Spahn — the powerful leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in the Bundestag — who was forced to step down following allegations of hypocrisy over his decision to have a child via surrogacy in the United States, circumventing German law and in violation of his party's principles.

Thorsten Frei: a Merz confidant

Thorsten Frei, previously the head of the chancellery, is now set to become the new leader of the conservative parliamentary group on Wednesday, which involves the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU). The 208 CDU and CSU lawmakers must cut their summer holidays short to vote on this appointment.

The 52-year-old Frei, currently serving as head of the chancellery and considered a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is now set to take over one of the most important positions in German politics. His task will be to explain his party's positions in speeches in the Bundestag and interviews with the media. Above all, he will have to secure majorities for the government's policies and negotiate with the conservatives' coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Nina Warken: a woman in a key position

Merz has a reputation for trusting only men within his inner circle. Now, 47-year-old Nina Warken — a politician from the wealthy southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg — is taking over from Frei and will manage the chancellery and be responsible for aligning the government's overall policy agenda.

Warken is a member of the women's organization of the Christian Democratic Union. As health minister, she had recently pushed through a cost-cutting program for statutory health insurance funds.

The chancellor considers Warken to be assertive and well-versed in security policy issues — an important quality, given that the head of the chancellery also coordinates oversight of Germany's intelligence agencies.

Carsten Linnemann: a health minister with a business focus

With Warken now leaving the health portfolio, Carsten Linnemann — previously the CDU general secretary — is set to take over.

Pundits argue that the chancellor certainly has a clear vision of how Linnemann should lead the department. Until now, Linnemann has been known primarily as an economics expert — a background that Friedrich Merz believes will serve him well in the new role: "Carsten Linnemann is taking over a ministry that represents the fastest-growing sector of our economy. The entire sector — which, unfortunately, we all too often view merely as a cost factor — is a vital part of our social fabric."

CDU politicians fear for September election prospects

Approval of the government's performance is at an all-time low. State elections are scheduled for September in three eastern states where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to see significant gains.

It is against this backdrop that Merz is demonstrating decisiveness.

"I assume that things will have calmed down somewhat by September," Merz said.

Sven Schulze (CDU), a minister in the Saxony-Anhalt state government, takes a very different view. Speaking to public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk on Monday, Schulze said the past few days had dominated political discussions and "not exactly gone well."

He added that it was almost impossible to focus on state-level issues during door-to-door campaigning in his state.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit
entries.summary: Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.
entries.content:
India

Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit

July 27, 2026

Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.

Walking from Jantar Mantar to Connaught Place in central New Delhi on Saturday evening provided an unusual sight for the prime corridor of power in the world's largest democracy.

Satirical posters mocking India's legislative, executive and judiciary were plastered on the walls, and the pavement was sprayed with sometimes "vulgar" graffiti mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

These were all remnants of thousands of young Cockroach movement protesters who had flooded the streets hours earlier after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Celebrating Pradhan's resignation, which had been a core protest demand, some protesters were heard telling security officials "see you at the next protest," coming only days after several people were injured in clashes with baton-wielding police who fired tear gas into crowds.

Instagram was also full of images from cities across India with young people dancing in front of police officials to the line "Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer " from Lana Del Ray's song "Playing Dangerous."

Others held posters reading: "Cuff me, daddy" and some were seen climbing atop police barricades.

India's Gen Z rattles government into change

The movement, known as the Cockroach Janta Party movement (CJP), came after the chief justice of India referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is also a play on Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Since a scandal broke in May involving a highly competitive university entrance exam, the Gen Z protests have spread across India, challenging the political establishment with Instagram reels, viral trends, sarcastic jingles and posters.

"In our generation humor has become the defense mechanism from pain, frustration and helplessness. This entire protest is driven by humor, driven by Instagram and social media," Karan Azad, a 24-year-old law student, told DW at the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Another protester held a sign addressed to Modi reading in transliterated Hindi: "Buddy, you can't even make tea," alluding to Modi's boyhood days as a tea seller.

"I had to do my part. I am the youth. If we don't stand up for ourselves no one else will, we have to fight this battle ourselves," the female protester with the sign told DW without giving her name.

A protester named Tushar, also 24, said he wasn't "afraid of a backlash" from the authorities, but rather "would have had FOMO [fear of missing out]" had he not joined the protest.

Ridhima, a 17-year-old school student, said: "If not us then who? Those who are not here, it just speaks to their cowardice and I am talking about people who are sitting on their chairs in positions of power."

What drove the Cockroach movement?

Content creator Arun Singh, known by his social media handle "TheJhumroo," said that meme culture kept the satire and humor fresh throughout the protests.

"It's the meme culture which fueled this kind of emotion. As millennials, we developed the language of memes as we adapted to the internet culture, but this younger generation was born with memes being their language. This is how they communicate," he told DW.

Singh said that the young protesters are best described as "fearless."

"They don't fear anyone, they don't worry about how they would be perceived and that's what happens when you're absolutely young. That is what is driving their grit," he said.

Mumbai-based comedian Aditi Mittal observes that the fearlessness of the Gen Z protesters comes from them living in a "hyper visible world".

"All of them have 500 followers at a minimum. If something goes up on their stories, it's not going to go vastly ignored," she told DW.

Mittal also thinks that India's Gen Z inherited the "perfect protest."

"The generation prior to ours wanted better infrastructure. We millennials aspired to have a more equal world, ours was a time distinct with, for example, the mistreatment of Muslims. We grew up in that and were constantly gaslit into… 'it's not that bad, it's not happening.' We were also overly forbearing," she told DW. "Gen Z inherited the perfect protest. Education goes beyond religion and secularism. It can resonate, especially for a country like ours where education has been the tool of escape from social class or a financial situation."

Mittal also points out differences between today and the 2019 citizenship law (CAA) protests, one of the last big protests that had challenged the Modi government, and was centered on discrimination against Muslims.

"The anti-CAA protests constantly demanded the perfection of the protesters. Be nice to them [authorities] even as they beat you or hold a gun to you, that was the language spoken to us. But these younger kids don't stand around and wait. They are not tripping over themselves to be perfect," she said.

Getting attention with political humor

Satire is not new to India's politics. For example, caricatures were used as a means to channel anti-colonial anger in Bengal. Political cartoonists like Abu Abraham and R K Laxman challenged censorship brought on by former Prime Minister and Congress leader Indira Gandhi's imposition of a state of emergency that suspended civil liberties between 1975 and 1977.

"Satire is a great way of putting your word across. It's like eating a healthy food, but cooked in an interesting way, which is munchable. Humor has better penetration when it comes to content. It gets more eyeballs," content creator Singh told DW.

Academic and writer Ananya Vajpeyi said that this sense of humor built sympathy with the students and kept the mood light and non-threatening.

"These were young boys and girls who looked tiny, not strong, not threatening, not even articulate sometimes, who had drawn or written something funny on a piece of paper. The violent crackdown backfired immediately because these were not two equal forces facing each other," she told DW.

India's Gen-Z rattles 'brand Modi'

Modi is seen as an image-conscious politician and his 12 years in India's seat of power have been defined by a carefully crafted image that relies heavily on perception management and public relations.

Many of the protesters directly mocked Modi, challenging his brand.

"The whole atmosphere has been so stifled since the anti-CAA protest was shut down. People have been punished for expressing any kind of criticism or dissent. And here you have thousands of students from every corner of the country, just like cockroaches crawling out of the woodwork and making life hell for the Modi establishment," Vajpeyi told DW.

Vajpeyi says the ire against Modi has likely caused "embarrassment" for the prime minister.

"What these kids are saying is like a punch in the stomach for Modi, if he is able to see all this. It's possible that he's being kept from it by those around him, but the opposition sees it," she said. "The rest of the country who is on social media sees it."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ghana's community service bill: A fix for the prison crisis?
entries.summary: The community service bill offers community service as an alternative to prison sentences, particularly for minor offenses. It's meant to decongest Ghana's prisons and prevent overcrowding once it's signed into law.
entries.content:
July 27, 2026

The community service bill offers community service as an alternative to prison sentences, particularly for minor offenses. It's meant to decongest Ghana's prisons and prevent overcrowding once it's signed into law.

Ghana's parliament recently passed the Community Service Bill, 2026. The piece of legislation is designed to introduce community service as an alternative to custodial sentences for minor offenses. The bill also seeks to ease pressure on the country's overcrowded prisons and reshape how justice is administered for minor crimes.

The legislation establishes a National Community Service Secretariat and provides a legal framework for courts to impose community service in Ghana instead of imprisonment for specified offenses.

According to the government, the move will reduce the financial strain of maintaining prison facilities, which have long suffered from inadequate budgets, high medical costs and chronic congestion.

"If you check the current prison population, overcrowding is over 37%. We have a current population of over 13,000 prisoners. Today the cost of maintaining them, feeding them alone, requires 10 million cedis (€752,000, $859,000)  a quarter," Ghana's Interior Minister, Muntaka Mubarak, who tabled the bill in parliament, told the house during a debate.

Which offenses are covered under the community service bill?

Under the bill, community service applies to offenses punishable by not more than three years' imprisonment, with or without a fine. Courts may also impose community service for offenses that carry fines alone or fines combined with imprisonment.

This means petty crimes such as false publication or traffic offenses could now attract noncustodial penalties.

Legal practitioner Christian Malm Hesse described the bill as "a step in the right direction," noting its potential to reduce prison overcrowding.

He told DW that the bill provides a structured alternative for misdemeanor offenses that previously defaulted to custodial sentences.

However, some Ghanaians believe that its effectiveness will depend on proper categorization of offenses and public education.

According to DW correspondent Eric Mawuena Egbeta, many Ghanaians still need clarity on which offenses qualify.

"An offense which is higher than a misdemeanor would mean that you will not get a community sentence… A lot more persons would need education on it," Egbeta said.

For legal practitioners like Hesse, one key safeguard in the bill is the requirement for a social inquiry report, which helps judges assess an offender's background, circumstances and suitability for community service. Hesse said such measures ensure that sentencing decisions are informed and consistent, reducing the risk of arbitrary application.

Africa's shift toward noncustodial sentencing

Ghana's new passage aligns with a growing trend across Africa, where countries such as Nigeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda have adopted similar noncustodial sentencing legislation.

International bodies, including the United NationsOffice on Drugs and Crime, have long encouraged alternatives to prison sentences, citing benefits such as reduced recidivism (where a person returns to criminal behavior and is sent back to jail after finishing a past sentence), lower state expenditure and improved community reintegration.

For Ghana, the bill represents the culmination of a decade-long policy process initiated in 2014 by the Ministry of the Interior with support from UNICEF.  The resulting framework aims to modernize justice administration and align national laws with global best practices on restorative justice.

Experts say the bill could be a game-changer for the continent, offering a model for balancing accountability with rehabilitation. By redirecting minor offenders toward community labor, skills development and civic responsibility, Ghana joins a broader African effort to rethink punishment beyond incarceration.

What do Ghanaians think about the bill?

Christabel Success, a Ghanaian journalist, said the law is "most appropriate for minor offenses," but stressed the need for fairness in its application.

"The method of application is what will determine whether it is a good bill or not," she told DW.

"It will help us with our capacity building, nation building and ridding our communities and our environment of waste," Nurah Suglo, an Accra-based resident, told DW.  

"We'd have cleaner cities, cleaner regions and make good use of our labor instead of overcrowding our prisons. People with minor offenses get to also do something that will contribute to the nation as a whole," Success added.

Egbeta, however, noted that crimes classified as second-degree felonies, such as stealing after breaking into a home, remain outside the bill's scope, which may disappoint those hoping for broader reforms. Although Parliament has passed the Community Service Bill, it cannot take effect until President John Dramani Mahama gives his assent.

Despite hailing its passage, Hesse explained that another crucial step for the bill is the creation of a Legislative Instrument (L.I).

"What is left is an L.I. When bills like this are passed, it becomes the secondary legislation under which operations become effective," Hesse said.

This article was adapted from an AfricaLink Podcast. You can listen to the podcast here.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu
